_comment: Ceilings and tolerances for tests/perf/gate.py. A metric fails when it is
over its platform's ceiling, when it is significantly slower than the base
commit at `alpha`, or when it is slower by more than `large_change`.
The ceilings are a backstop for a run with no base to compare with (a
main push, a manual run). They sit close to what the runners do, to keep
Chanto's lead rather than only catch disasters. CPU time per run varies by
up to 2.6x between GitHub's runner instances, so CPU ceilings sit about 1.3
times the slowest run seen (October 30-31, 2026: startup / per request at
most Linux 21.9 / 2.5 ms, macOS 35 / 4.2 ms, Windows per request 16 ms).
Windows startup sits at 90 ms: #168 cut it, only a few runs follow (slowest
46.9 ms, 93.8 ms before it), and its clock ticks every 15.6 ms. Peak memory
is stable, so about 1.1 times (startup / 40 turns: Linux 18.9 / 20.5 MB,
macOS 17.1 / 18.8 MB, Windows 14.8 / 17.1 MB). A failure on a change that
costs nothing means a slower runner than these saw: rerun it before raising
a ceiling. The comparison with the base, on the same runner, holds a change.
reps: startup runs are cheap and noisy, so there are more of them; the
turn workload is a whole session each but still costs a second, next to
two eight-minute builds. With 50 and 15 samples the U test reaches
alpha=0.01 when about 64% (startup) or 75% (turns) of one set sits above
the other, so a 10% shift
against ~1% run-to-run noise is caught with room to spare. Startup was 20
runs, whose median a few milliseconds of jitter on a busy macOS runner
moved by 15% with the code unchanged. warmup runs are discarded.
tolerance: below this change a metric is never called a regression.
alpha: the one-sided Mann-Whitney U test on the two sample sets.
large_change: fails even without a significant p-value, if p is under
large_change_p: the sets must at least lean apart. Noise that moved only
the median gives p near 0.3; a real 10-30% shift, well under 0.001.
device: the same 40-turn workload pinned to `cpus` core against wall-time
and memory ceilings, for a machine with no spare cores and a phone's
memory. It has no base to compare with, since wall time on a shared
runner measures the runner; the ceilings sit about 1.3 times the slowest of
20 runs (244.5 / 4.6 ms) and 1.1 times for memory (20.7 MB).
binary_mb: the release binary's size, in 10^6 bytes. It is exact, so it
has no tolerance or test: it fails only over its ceiling, and a pull
request that needs more raises the ceiling here, where reviewers see the
growth. About 2.5% above the builds of October 31, 2026
(macOS 20.3, Linux 24.0, Windows 29.3 MB).
tests/perf/stress.py: a long session and a large tree, against the fake
model. Ceilings from the last 16 Linux and macOS runs (October 31, 2026:
long session 39.5 MB, large tree 32 MB, resume 25.5 MB and 0.15 s): about
1.25 times for memory and 1.5-3 times for step times, which vary more on a
shared runner. drift:
the last quarter's median gap between model requests may be at most
this times the first quarter's, plus 2 ms.
grep_vs_rg: Grep for paths may take at most this times `rg -l` on the
same tree, plus 0.3 s; a search forced onto one thread is not.
tests/perf/exact.py, on Linux: instruction counts and prompt size. First
values, to be set from what the runners report.
